items.title: The Apprentice Who Outgrew the Shop
items.pitch: Invest in a struggling clothing store and give its future apprentice a way in. The thriving shop you create may eventually be the one that replaces your original beneficiary.

present_hook.what_you_notice: An old clothing store has an empty second workbench; an archived notice shows that the owner once tried to hire help and withdrew the offer.

clues.line: {A} withdrew the hiring notice in {year}. The second workbench was never put to use.

window.notes: shop belongs to A. Require the baseline withdrawn hiring notice, a vacant dress-shop site and sufficient local demand for a viable new entrant. B is an unrelated eligible worker. Present must be at least 26 years later.

interventions.how_it_looks: Fund the unused workbench and the payroll needed for a second worker.

ripples.headline: Second Workbench Finally Gets a Worker
ripples.body: {A} hired {B} at the clothing store. A shelved expansion plan finally reached the cutting table.

ripples.headline: Former Apprentice Opens a Competing Dress Shop
ripples.body: {B} opened a dress shop after years of paid work and training. The independent venture put a strain on relations with former employer {A}.

ripples.headline: Original Clothing Store Closes as Rival Thrives
ripples.body: The clothing store run by {A} closed after losing trade to the dress shop founded by {B}. The new proprietor's success left an older workroom empty.

fails.headline: Expansion Money Fails to Produce the Promised Job
fails.body: The clothing store run by {A} spent its expansion money without creating the advertised position. The unfilled workbench became a source of local disappointment.

present_day.best: In {now}, the original clothing-store doorway is boarded after its recorded closure, while the competing dress-shop premises have been created; later use and ownership follow replay.
present_day.worst: If the first step fails, no apprentice or competing shop is guaranteed. The investment has still been spent under business accounting.
present_day.twist: The investment succeeds at teaching a trade and creating independence, but the teacher loses the original store to the pupil's competition.

npc_lines_after.line: I taught those hands to make a living. I just did not expect it to cost me mine.

new_rules_needed: Use keyed RNG per seed, scenario ID, intervention year, roles and step; choose each event year within its after_years range measured from intervention. Roll only after eligibility passes. Steps 2 and 3 require their predecessor; failure stops descendants without undoing earlier effects. fails is the complementary first-step result, never a separate roll; ineligibility produces no failure headline. Recheck survival, residence, ownership, budgets and sites. Apply interventions once, keep world facts separate from beliefs, persist object/building IDs and invalidate dependent history on replay. Do not force later survival or ownership. Present descriptions require the recorded outcome and surviving map features; named after-speakers must be alive. No repeat rewards.

Step 1 requires A's open store, a real funded vacancy and B available for employment. Investment credits business capital once; failure spends that capital on recorded unsuccessful expansion rather than subtracting the player's transfer again.

Step 2 requires actual training, saved earnings, B's adult business eligibility and a funded vacant site. End B's old employment before founding; record a competitive customer overlap, not magical theft of wealth.

Step 3 requires A still owning shop, B owning the open scenario dress shop and sustained operating losses from the recorded customer overlap. Close shop through insolvency accounting; the 20 percent wealth loss is the defined personal debt settlement, not a second copy of business losses. Gate the after-line on step 3, A's survival and no later recovery of the original store.
items.era_notes: Use paper patterns and fitting appointments throughout; avoid claims that a particular fabric or machine exists in every decade.
items.why_fun: You can meet the apprentice before the opportunity and walk past both storefronts after it. Helping someone become independent can be uncomfortable.

items.title: Bread Behind the Vault Door
items.pitch: Sabotage a bank that keeps refusing a baker's lease proposal. The empty building may become a neighborhood bakery, but the missing bank will still matter to people who needed it.

present_hook.what_you_notice: A bank occupies a former shopfront, and a rejected bakery lease application survives in the archive. Its vault door is visible from the lobby.

clues.line: {B} proposed a bakery here in {year}. The bank would not release the building.

window.notes: shop is A's bank. Require the rejected bakery lease, an otherwise solvent bank that sabotage can push below its closure threshold, recorded bank employees and a deposit-protection mechanism. Present must be at least 27 years later.

interventions.how_it_looks: Undermine the bank's business prospects during the year its building lease is being renewed.

ripples.headline: Bank Closes, Leaving Its Vault and Staff Behind
ripples.body: The bank operated by {A} closed after a severe business setback. Employees lost their positions while protected deposits entered the settlement process.

ripples.headline: Bakery Opens in the Former Bank
ripples.body: {B} opened a bakery inside the former bank after buying and converting the premises. The old vault door remained as an expensive cupboard entrance.

ripples.headline: Former Bank Bakery Adds a Production Wing
ripples.body: The bakery founded by {B} opened a production wing funded from its accumulated surplus. The preserved vault door now opens onto flour storage.

fails.headline: Bank Absorbs Setback and Keeps Its Doors Open
fails.body: {A} covered the bank's losses from personal funds. The building remained unavailable to the proposed bakery.

present_day.best: In {now}, a bakery building and its production wing occupy the former bank site, with the vault door preserved inside. Check ordinary replay before promising a still-operating bakery.
present_day.worst: On first-step failure, the bank survives the sabotage and no scenario bakery follows. A has still paid for the damage.
present_day.twist: A destructive intervention gives the town bread and a useful building conversion. It also removes bank jobs and a nearby banking counter; protected deposits do not replace those services.

npc_lines_after.line: The bread smells wonderful. I used to come through that door for a wage.

Require deposit protection or a complete explicit settlement rule before activating: closure transfers protected accounts without erasing residents' money. Record staff dismissals and loss of local counter service. The employee after-line requires an actual surviving former employee of shop.

Sabotage changes business prospects once. Step 1 is the conditional consequence of that setback; its closure must not be applied again by a separate insolvency event. Failure's wealth loss represents A's recorded recapitalization payment.

Reserve the closed building ID after step 1; step 2 requires a lawful completed purchase, sufficient B funds, food-business approval and no intervening occupant. Preserve the vault door as an identified map object.

Step 3 requires B's open solvent bakery, sufficient saved business capital, expansion permission and a vacant adjacent plot reserved at activation. Debit construction costs before creating the wing. The former-employee line additionally requires step 3 and no restored bank service at this site.
items.era_notes: Use generic banking and baking equipment. Do not imply nationwide deposit protections existed identically in every decade; use the explicit world settlement rule.
items.why_fun: A cruel shortcut creates a welcoming destination with an unmistakable remnant of what you destroyed. Former employees can remember the same doorway differently.

items.title: A House for Two Late Beginnings
items.pitch: Introduce two older strangers who keep declining invitations. A late marriage could create a more accessible home, then turn an abandoned family house into a public reading room.

present_hook.what_you_notice: Two separate homes have notices offering spare chairs, while a nearby cottage plot remains unused. Archived invitations show that their residents never attended the same gathering.

clues.line: {A} and {B} each offered a spare chair in {year}. Their names never appeared on the same guest list.

window.notes: B is a stranger to A. Require both owning separate homes outright with no other occupants, an available accessible-cottage plot on Main Street and consent to eventual public reuse of A's house. Present must be at least 23 years later; do not guarantee either resident survives that long.

interventions.how_it_looks: Arrange one afternoon visit with two spare chairs and an ordinary pot of tea.

ripples.headline: Two Spare Chairs Become a Shared Table
ripples.body: {A} and {B} married after a friendship begun over afternoon tea. They asked guests to bring company rather than presents.

ripples.headline: Late-Life Couple Builds a Home Without Stairs
ripples.body: {A} and {B} moved into a shared cottage designed without entrance steps. Their former houses were left empty pending agreed future uses.

effects.tear_down: the unoccupied former house of A

ripples.headline: Former Family House Gives Way to a Reading Room
ripples.body: {A} and {B} funded a public reading room on the site of the old house of {A}. The original porch was removed during construction.

fails.headline: New Acquaintances Choose Friendship Over Marriage
fails.body: {A} and {B} remained friendly after their introduction but chose separate households. Both described the acquaintance as welcome.

present_day.best: In {now}, a shared accessible cottage and public reading room exist on Main Street. The old house and porch of {A} are gone; current residents and later building use follow the replay.
present_day.worst: First-step failure still produces a modest friendship, but no scenario marriage, cottage or reading room. If either resident dies later, stop dependent steps rather than resurrecting them.
present_day.twist: Public readers gain a room and the couple gains an easier home, but A's original porch and household setting become irretrievable. A useful public gift can erase a private place.

npc_lines_after.line: I can reach the new door without climbing a step. I still remember how the old porch sounded.

Roll only after eligibility passes. Steps 2 and 3 require their predecessor; failure stops descendants without undoing earlier effects. fails is the complementary first-step result, never a separate roll; ineligibility produces no failure headline. Recheck survival, residence, ownership, budgets and sites. Apply interventions once, keep world facts separate from beliefs, persist object/building IDs and invalidate dependent history on replay. Do not force later survival or ownership. Present descriptions require the recorded outcome and surviving map features; named after-speakers must be alive. No repeat rewards.

Home ownership, occupancy, the reserved cottage parcel and A's former house on Main Street must be concrete baseline facts; no additional family members are evicted. Marriage requires both still unmarried, consenting and mutually eligible.

Step 2 requires the marriage intact and a funded lawful building plan. Debit pooled savings, build the cottage and atomically update both household residence IDs. Retain ownership of both emptied houses; reject if a later occupant or lien makes the plan impossible.

Step 3 requires both alive, still married, still occupying the cottage, still owning A's empty house and enough funds and public approval for the reading room. Demolition and construction are atomic; do not clear an occupied home. This deliberately rare long-survival chain grants no immunity. Gate A's line on completed step 3, A alive and the cottage still accessible.
items.era_notes: Use generic accessible housing features and printed reading material. A late marriage is possible in every listed decade; do not assume a deceased former spouse.
items.why_fun: The first payoff is a shared doorstep rather than a dynasty. Repeated visits reveal how a happy ending can still leave a place worth mourning.

items.title: The Boot That Founded Nothing
items.pitch: Plant an imitation relic where a local history enthusiast will find it. A joke can acquire a monument before the town finally discovers that its founding artifact never belonged to its founder.

present_hook.what_you_notice: An empty display case stands in the church hall beside an unsigned proposal for a town-founder monument. A clipping describes an excavation that found nothing worth keeping.

clues.line: {A} searched the old cellar in {year}. The proposed founder display stayed empty.

window.notes: A and B are unrelated residents. Require a scheduled cellar excavation, an empty public display case, B's recorded interest in monument patronage and a vacant civic plinth on Main Street. Present must be at least 27 years later.

interventions.how_it_looks: Hide an imitation old boot with a false founder label in the cellar before the recorded excavation.

ripples.headline: Cellar Find Offered as a Founder Relic
ripples.body: {A} displayed a boot found beneath an old cellar and proposed that it belonged to a town founder. The attribution has not been independently verified.

ripples.headline: Patron Funds a Monument to a Disputed Boot
ripples.body: {B} funded a boot-shaped monument inspired by the cellar find. Its inscription adopted the founder attribution despite unanswered questions.

ripples.headline: Imitation Exposed; Boot Monument Removed
ripples.body: A comparison of materials and labels established that the supposed founder's boot was an imitation. The monument was removed, leaving its plinth and an embarrassing gap in the civic account.

fails.headline: Careful Excavator Rejects a Suspicious Boot
fails.body: {A} identified the planted boot as a modern imitation before offering it for display. The empty case remained empty, and the failed hoax earned the excavator praise.

present_day.best: In {now}, the plinth is empty again, but mounting scars and a correction plaque record the removed boot monument. The hoax is documented as false rather than becoming true through repetition.
present_day.worst: If step 1 succeeds and step 2 succeeds but step 3 fails, the monument remains and its false attribution continues as a belief; museum and NPC truth records still mark the object as an imitation.
present_day.twist: The hoax gives the town a conversation piece and a generous public donation, then damages the reputations of the enthusiast and patron. Exposing it restores the record but removes a sculpture residents may have liked.

npc_lines_after.line: The boot is gone. People still give directions by it.

proposed_verbs.does: Create one player-carried imitation-boot object at the reserved cellar site before its scheduled excavation, consuming that inventory object. Record actual manufacture date and false label separately from observers' beliefs. Planting neither changes history before placement nor guarantees discovery, acceptance or a monument.

new_rules_needed: Use keyed RNG per seed, scenario ID, intervention year, roles and step; choose each event year within its after_years range measured from intervention. Roll only after eligibility passes. Steps 2 and 3 require their predecessor; failure stops descendants without undoing earlier effects. fails is the complementary first-step result, never a separate roll; ineligibility produces no failure headline. Recheck survival, residence, ownership, budgets and sites. Apply interventions once, keep world facts separate from beliefs, persist object/building IDs and invalidate dependent history on replay. Do not force later survival or ownership. Present descriptions require the recorded outcome and surviving map features; named after-speakers must be alive. No repeat rewards.

Require the player to possess the specified imitation object. Step 1 includes deterministic discovery during the scheduled excavation and mistaken attribution; its complementary failure records A's detection of the imitation. If A is dead or excavation is cancelled, leave the planted object in the world without inventing either headline.

Step 2 requires the active false_founder_boot thread, an accepted public proposal, B's consent and a construction quote no greater than 20 percent of B's current wealth. The wealth effect is the entire earmarked donation; do not charge it twice. Keep the existing plinth beneath the new monument.

Step 3 requires surviving object evidence, access for a qualified investigator and the monument still present. Identification establishes the true materials through a recorded examination, resolves the thread and removes only the boot sculpture. Preserve the plinth, mounting scars and an explicit correction plaque as map state; this plaque annotation is part of the resolution rule. Reputation changes for deceased A or B apply only to historical reputation records, never resurrected residents.

The worst description applies only to the step-3 roll failure after the first two successes. Other partial outcomes use actual history. Gate the after-line on completed step 3, surviving plinth evidence and a resident who knows the old landmark.
items.era_notes: Use physical labels and material inspection rather than assuming digital forensic equipment. The founder remains unnamed and generated history determines whether any real founder artifact exists.
items.why_fun: You manufacture the uncanny clue rather than merely discover it. The full chain ends with an empty place that means something different from the empty place you started with.
